title: Fewest Arrow Flips From Every Root
statement:
There are n nodes numbered 0 to n − 1 and n − 1 one-way edges. edges[i] = [u, v] is an arrow from u to v. If you ignore the directions, the edges form a tree.

For a chosen start node, you may flip arrows so that every node can be reached from the start by following arrows. For every node i, find the fewest flips needed when i is the start. Return the answers as an array answer of length n. Each start is a separate question: flips for one start do not carry over to another.

examples.why: The path is 0 – 1 – 2 – 3. From 1, only 3 → 2 points the wrong way. From 3, only 1 → 2 does. From 0 or 2, two arrows point back toward the start.
From 0 everything is already reachable. From 1, the arrow 0 → 1 must be flipped to get back to 0; then 0 → 2 works as is.
All arrows point toward 0. Moving the start one step toward 4 fixes exactly one more arrow.

constraints: The edges form a tree when directions are ignored
hints: Solve it for one start first. Which arrows must be flipped when the tree hangs from node 0?
From node 0, every arrow that points toward the root must flip. Now move the start from a node to its neighbour. Which single arrow changes its status?

Only the arrow between the old and the new start changes: if it pointed old → new it now needs a flip (+1), if it pointed new → old it no longer does (−1). Compute the answer for 0 with one DFS, then push answers to children with a second pass.

explain.intuition:
Fix a start and hang the tree from it. Every node must be reached by walking away from the start, so each arrow must point away from the start. The answer is the number of arrows pointing toward it. One DFS from node 0 counts that for node 0.

Running that DFS from every node costs O(n²). Instead, compare two neighbouring starts p and c. Every arrow except the one between them faces the same way relative to both starts, because moving the start across one edge does not change which side of the rest of the tree any other edge lies on. So answer[c] = answer[p] + 1 if the arrow is p → c (fine before, wrong now), and answer[p] − 1 if it is c → p. This is called rerooting: one pass to get the root's answer, a second pass to slide it to every node.
steps: Build an undirected adjacency list. For an arrow u → v, store (v, 0) at u (free to walk) and (u, 1) at v (walking it needs a flip).
Traverse from node 0 and add up the costs of the edges used: that is answer[0].
Traverse again from 0. For each step from parent p to child c with cost w, set answer[c] = answer[p] + (w == 0 ? 1 : −1).
Return answer. Use an explicit stack or queue, since a path of 100 000 nodes overflows recursion.
pitfalls: Getting the sign backwards when moving the start. An arrow p → c was free for start p and needs a flip for start c, so the answer goes up.
Using recursion on a long path. The tree can be a chain of 100 000 nodes.
Treating the graph as directed when building the adjacency list. You must be able to walk every edge in both directions to visit the whole tree.

solutions.title: Count from every start
solutions.idea: For each start, walk the whole tree and count the edges walked against their arrow.

solutions.title: Reroot from node 0
solutions.idea: Count flips for start 0, then move the start across one edge at a time: only that edge's status changes.

followups: Return only the start that needs the fewest flips. Can you avoid computing every answer?
The underlying graph may have cycles. Why does the rerooting trick break?
lcTitle: Minimum Edge Reversals So Every Node Is Reachable
